analysis.one_liner: Requires big automakers to sell thousands of new cars each year with anti-drunk-driving technology.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 18, 2025, and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee; it has no cosponsors and no action since referral [S1][S3][S4].
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require manufacturers that sell more than 250,000 vehicles a year in the U.S. to put at least 10,000 vehicles per year with drunk-driving detection technology (the DADSS system) and 10,000 vehicles per year meeting European safety standards for driver monitoring on the market [S2]. It would take effect 180 days after enactment and expire once the federal rule required by the 2021 infrastructure law mandating this technology in all new cars takes effect [S2]. The bill is named for the Abbas family, killed by a drunk driver in Michigan.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who shares the road with drunk drivers. Drunk driving kills roughly 13,000 people a year in the U.S., and passive alcohol-detection systems are designed to detect an impaired driver and stop or limit the vehicle. The bill would force early deployment of that technology rather than waiting for the slower federal rulemaking process.

how_it_helps.text: Large automakers would have to sell or import at least 10,000 vehicles per year that meet the DADSS performance specifications — technology that detects an impaired driver — and at least 10,000 vehicles per year meeting European New Car Assessment Programme driver-monitoring standards [S2].

The requirement would start within 180 days of enactment, meaning deployment would not wait on federal rulemaking, and violations would carry the same civil penalties as other federal vehicle safety standard violations [S2].

The mandate is designed as a bridge: it expires once the rule required under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act — which mandates impaired-driving prevention technology in new vehicles — takes effect [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Automakers selling more than 250,000 vehicles a year in the U.S. would bear the cost of installing the detection systems in at least 20,000 vehicles annually, a cost likely passed partly to buyers of those specific vehicles. The rest of the market would be unaffected by this bill.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large automakers and buyers of those vehicles

drawbacks.text: The bill is a blunt instrument: it sets fixed numeric quotas (10,000 vehicles each for two standards) rather than a percentage of production or a performance deadline, which may be easy for manufacturers to satisfy at the margin without meaningfully changing fleet-wide safety [S2].
Installing advanced impairment-detection systems costs money, and manufacturers would likely pass some of that cost to buyers of the affected vehicles, at least initially [S2].
If the federal rule required by the infrastructure law is delayed, the temporary mandate could last longer than the 'bridge' framing suggests, since it only expires when that rule takes effect [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside — technology that can stop impaired drivers before they kill — is significant, and the cost is limited because the mandate applies to only 20,000 vehicles a year from each large manufacturer, a small share of production for companies selling 250,000-plus. The main honest criticism is design, not principle: fixed quotas are a weak lever, and automakers could comply in name while the technology reaches few real-world drivers. The bill is a reasonable interim step toward the existing federal mandate, though a stronger version would scale the requirement to total production.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in mid-December 2025 and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no cosponsors, and no vote so far.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the bill on December 18, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S4].
As of the latest record, no other House member has cosponsored the bill [S3].
No further action appears in the bill's history after the committee referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No final outcome yet. So far, the benefit of inaction goes to large automakers, which face no new anti-drunk-driving mandate while the bill sits without a sponsor besides its author.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers, so far — no new mandate yet

for.name: Rep. Debbie Dingell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, named for the Abbas family killed by a drunk driver, and referred it to Energy and Commerce.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no other member has cosponsored, so there is no record of partisan support or opposition yet [S3].

industries.industry: Automakers selling more than 250,000 vehicles a year in the U.S.
industries.note: The bill requires these manufacturers to install impairment-detection and driver-monitoring technology in at least 20,000 vehicles per year, a compliance cost they would otherwise avoid until the federal rule under the infrastructure law takes effect [S2]. The industry's interest in blocking the requirement conflicts with the public's interest in vehicles that can stop impaired drivers, though the same industry will eventually have to install the technology fleet-wide under the infrastructure law, so this is a timing-and-cost fight rather than a fight over the technology itself.

A guaranteed annual market of at least 10,000 vehicles per large manufacturer for drunk-driving detection systems gives the companies developing this technology early production volumes and real-world data before a fleet-wide mandate [S2].

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been in committee for weeks with zero cosponsors, which is the profile of a bill that rarely reaches the floor. Unless Dingell builds cosponsor support or attaches the provision to a larger vehicle-safety package, it is likely to die in the Energy and Commerce Committee when this Congress ends in January 2027. The underlying technology requirement already exists in federal law with a delayed rule, so momentum for early deployment would have to come from members willing to pressure automakers.
